To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
F. asiatica survives and replicates in tilapia macrophages and that the survival and replication are dependent on iglC.
the iglC mutant of F. asiatica was unable to replicate and cause cytotoxicity to tilapia macrophages, but this was restored when the mutant was complemented with the intact iglC gene.

Francisella asiatica is resistant to tilapia serum, can be taken up by macrophages via complement and mannose receptor-dependent mechanisms, is able to replicate and induce cytotoxicity, and that the iglC mutant strain is defective for replication, survival, and cytotoxicity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interaction of F. asiatica with the fish innate immune system, which may be useful in the development of a live attenuated vaccine for the control of this fish pathogen.
understanding the pathogenic mechanisms involved in F. asiatica infection and the role of the iglC mutant in this infection.
the identification of genes and the mechanism(s) by which Francisella asiatica survives and replicates within tilapia macrophages.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the FPI is important for the interaction of F. asiatica with tilapia macrophages.
the iglC mutant is defective for survival and intracellular replication in tilapia HKDM and that the igl gene products are required for intracellular survival of F. asiatica.

the FPI of F. asiatica contributes to the intracellular survival of the bacterium in HKDM and is important for cytotoxicity and apoptosis induction in these cells, but it is not important for the invasion process of the bacterium.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the iglC mutant is attenuated in its virulence and is a good candidate for the development of a Francisella asiatica subunit vaccine.
F. asiatica has the ability to resist serum killing, invade HKDM, survive, replicate, and cause macrophage apoptosis.

the iglC mutant of F. asiatica, which is deficient for survival in HKDM, was complemented with iglC, resulting in the ability of the mutant strain to survive in HKDM, which indicates that IglC is important for F. asiatica survival in HKDM.
The main takeaway from our work is that
F. asiatica can invade tilapia macrophages, replicate, cause cytotoxicity, and induce apoptosis.
the iglC mutant is unable to cause cytotoxic effects and apoptosis in HKDM and that the F. asiatica iglABCD genes are important for the survival and replication of F. asiatica in tilapia macrophages.
the iglC mutant is attenuated in the fish macrophages and is a potential vaccine candidate against Francisella asiatica.
